passages.original: venio nunc longo sane intervallo ad quandam epistulam, qua mihi multa tribuens unum reprehendebas quod in honoribus decernendis essem nimius et tamquam prodigus. tu hoc; alius fortasse, quod in animadversione poenaque durior, nisi forte utrumque tu. quod si ita est, utriusque rei meum iudicium studeo tibi esse notissimum †neque solum ut Solonis dictum usurpem† qui et sapientissimus fuit ex septem et legum scriptor solus ex septem. is rem publicam contineri duabus rebus dixit, praemio et poena. est scilicet utriusque rei modus sicut reliquarum et quaedam in utroque genere mediocritas.
passages.english: I come now, after a long interval indeed, to a certain letter of yours, in which, while granting me much, you found fault with one thing: that in voting honours I was excessive and, as it were, prodigal. You [say] this; someone else perhaps [says] that in reprimand and punishment I am too harsh, unless perhaps you [say] both. If that is so, I am eager that my judgement on each of these matters should be very well known to you, †and not only so that I may cite the saying of Solon,† who was both the wisest of the Seven and the only lawgiver among the Seven. He said that the state is held together by two things, reward and punishment. There is, of course, a measure in each of these, as in everything else, and a certain mean in each kind.
passages.notes: The clause 'neque solum ut Solonis dictum usurpem' is marked by the edition as corrupt (obelised); the sense of 'not only' is unclear and the translation is literal. 'The Seven' are the Seven Sages of Greece.
